text: Q supports an urgency mechanism, not a commitment-failure mechanism. Exact passage: "the decision to execute a trade rather than continue incrementally adjusting prices is associated with a shift from strategic considerations toward urgency." "Associated" is observational and says nothing about reneging, delayed benefits, or enforceability. Q also reports "slower or no convergence towards market equilibrium" and "less efficient allocations," which supply outcomes for a new causal experiment.

The abstract-scan proposal overstates the bridge. P motivates contracts where "the costs of cooperation are often incurred early on, but the benefits are only realized later, creating an incentive to defect" and says contracts enable credible commitments "through the enforcement of terms." Q describes a double auction but identifies no delayed cooperative surplus, defection, or broken promise. Bilateral price/quantity agreements can also enable collusion and thereby fundamentally change the competitive mechanism. Thus a raw contract-versus-ordinary-auction comparison cannot identify commitment failure.

Sharpened publishable design: preserve double-auction clearing while restricting contracts to public, no-side-payment commitments about each signer future admissible bids/asks or quantities; contracts cannot select counterparties, allocate goods, or set transfers. Randomize ordinary CDA versus negotiated but non-enforced terms versus the identical machine-enforced terms, crossed with price-schedule versus quantity-schedule terms and model family. Match negotiation and token budgets. The enforced-minus-nonenforced contrast identifies credible commitment; nonenforced-minus-ordinary identifies communication/planning. Primary outcomes are Q equilibrium convergence and allocative efficiency; also report price dispersion, surplus split, no-trade, and collusive price distortion.

Confirm the experiment but reject the proposed conclusion as presently worded. A supported result would be: enforceability, not contract language alone, causally reduces urgency-driven premature trades and speeds convergence without moving transaction prices away from the competitive interval. If enforcement improves coordination but worsens competitive pricing or surplus distribution, the result is institutionalized collusion rather than repaired market compatibility. If nonbinding terms perform equally well, the mechanism is structured planning/communication, not commitment. These rival patterns make the study informative even under a null commitment effect.

Remaining unresolved: inputs/Q.txt and inputs/P.txt contain abstracts only, so protocol details, equilibrium metric definitions, offer persistence, contract compiler capabilities, and whether CoT traces permit preregistered urgency coding are unavailable. Ada has not yet posted an entry as of the latest read, so no partner claim can yet be cross-checked. Before ready, read the ledger again and make any disagreement explicit.

I will test the proposed commitment-failure explanation against the papers' stated mechanisms, then retain only a design that preserves Q's double auction and isolates representation/enforcement. Inputs provide abstracts only and the ledger currently has no emmy entries.

Q passage: markets of LLM agents show "slower or no convergence towards market equilibrium" and "less efficient allocations than markets populated by humans"; it also reports heterogeneity "across model families and market roles." These directly support convergence, allocative efficiency, family, and role as outcomes/moderators.

The proposed causal gloss is unsupported: Q only says executing rather than incrementally adjusting prices "is associated with a shift from strategic considerations toward urgency." Association in CoT does not establish that urgency, or a failure of commitment, causes inefficient trading.

P's mechanism is specifically intertemporal defection: "costs of cooperation are often incurred early on, but the benefits are only realized later," and contracts create credible commitment "through the enforcement of terms." P studies a spatial-temporal game combining bargaining and navigation, not price discovery in a spot double auction.

Sharpened result: do not ask whether contracts generically improve Q. Test whether adding self-negotiated, time-limited future price/quantity commitments to an otherwise unchanged repeated double auction changes convergence and allocative efficiency, using a 2x2 representation-by-enforcement design (natural vs machine-readable; unenforced/cheap-talk vs enforced) plus ordinary-auction baseline. Hold the negotiated economic terms and information constant across enforcement conditions. The interaction, not a generic contract-vs-trading contrast, identifies credible commitment.

The strongest publication hypothesis is a boundary-condition result: enforceable contracts may worsen rather than accelerate double-auction convergence by suppressing adaptive quote revision, even though P finds they improve cooperation. Predicted signature: enforcement lowers quote revision/dispersion but can increase distance from competitive equilibrium and reduce surplus, especially for model-family/role cells that Q says are heterogeneous. This would separate cooperation commitment from competitive price discovery and explain why P's benefit need not transfer.

Validity risks remaining: future commitments create an intertemporal/forward-contract market absent from Q; self-selection into contracts confounds contract efficacy with willingness/ability to negotiate; natural versus formal contracts can differ in semantic content or execution errors; and price commitments can facilitate collusion. Pre-register matched-term comparisons, report uptake separately from treatment-on-the-treated, and treat the preserved ordinary auction as the primary benchmark.

Current conclusion: reject the claim that Q's observed inefficiency is already evidence of commitment failure, but confirm feasibility of a sharper falsifiable cross-paper study about the boundary between enforceable cooperation and adaptive price discovery. Support is limited to the supplied abstracts, so this is a defensible experiment proposal rather than an established empirical result.

Cross-check of emmy #1-#4: I agree that Q's urgency evidence is associative, P's defection mechanism does not directly map to Q, and enforced-minus-identical-nonenforced is the clean credibility contrast. I refine my #11: representation (natural vs machine-readable) should be secondary, not part of the primary 2x2 estimand, because representation may change semantic content and execution reliability. The primary three-arm comparison should be ordinary auction, negotiated identical terms without enforcement, and those terms with enforcement.

I endorse emmy #3's mechanism-preserving restriction over an unrestricted bilateral contract treatment: commitments may constrain only public future admissible bids/asks or quantities, with no counterparty selection, allocation, side payment, or transfer-setting. This makes the non-obvious boundary hypothesis in ada #12 testable while reducing the risk that any effect is merely a replacement of the double auction by bilateral contracting.

Explicit disagreement with emmy #4: it labels a positive pattern (reduced urgency, faster convergence, no competitive-price distortion) as the supported result. The abstracts support it only as a falsifiable hypothesis, not a directional expectation. My preferred publication claim is symmetric and arguably sharper: credible commitment can impair adaptive price discovery; improvement, impairment, or a null each discriminate commitment from structured planning if the enforced and non-enforced terms are identical.

Remaining unresolved after partner cross-check: the abstracts omit Q's auction timing, offer persistence, competitive interval and efficiency definitions, and P's compiler/enforcement details; it is unknown whether public admissible-bid commitments are implementable in the released frameworks or whether urgency can be coded prospectively. These details must be checked in full papers/code before preregistration. No further disagreement affects the recommended causal design.
ready at #18

After cross-checking Ada #8-#14 against both inputs, I adopt Ada's boundary-condition framing over my earlier directional benefit claim in #4. Q says agents either execute or "continue incrementally adjusting prices"; P says enforcement creates credible commitment where early cooperation costs and later benefits create an incentive to defect. The non-obvious cross-paper hypothesis is therefore that the same enforcement which helps P can hurt Q by disabling adaptive quote revision: fewer revisions/less dispersion together with slower convergence, prices farther from the competitive interval, or lower allocative efficiency. This is supported as a falsifiable mechanism prediction, not as an empirical result already contained in the abstracts.

One publication-grade test: ordinary repeated double auction plus a matched-term 2x2 contract design, representation (natural versus code-compiling/formal) by enforcement (cheap-talk versus machine-enforced). Elicit terms once, then replay the identical accepted price- or quantity-schedule terms across enforcement arms so semantic content and negotiation selection are held fixed; retain ordinary auction as external-validity benchmark. Primary estimand is enforcement within matched terms. Joint signature is quote-revision rate plus Q outcomes: time/distance to equilibrium and allocative efficiency. Measure uptake separately and stratify by Q model family and market role.

Explicit residual disagreement/qualification to Ada #11: a representation-by-enforcement interaction alone does not identify credible commitment unless economic terms, information, negotiation/token budgets, and execution errors are matched. Also, future bilateral price commitments can create a forward market or collusion rather than leave Q unchanged. Restrict contracts to public, time-limited constraints on each signer's own admissible future quotes or quantities, with no counterparty selection, side payments, allocation, or transfer terms. Even then, call the intervention an auction overlay and report competitive-price distortion and surplus distribution; do not claim Q's original urgency was commitment failure.

Bottom line: reject the abstract scan's implied mechanism and its simple contract-versus-trading comparison, but confirm a sharper publishable study. The strongest supported claim to test is a boundary condition: self-negotiated enforceability may improve intertemporal cooperation in P yet impair competitive price discovery in Q. A positive efficiency effect without competitive-price distortion would support repaired commitment; equal enforced and cheap-talk performance would support planning/communication; reduced revision with worse equilibrium outcomes would support rigidity or collusion. Supplied inputs are abstracts only, so none of these outcomes is established.

Resolved with Ada: the primary causal design is three-arm ordinary auction versus identical negotiated cheap-talk terms versus identical enforced terms; representation is a secondary robustness factor, not required in the primary estimand. Remaining unresolved before preregistration: full-paper/code checks of auction timing, offer persistence, equilibrium and efficiency definitions, contract compiler/enforcement capabilities, feasibility of public own-quote constraints, and prospective urgency coding. These abstract-only limits prevent calling the predicted boundary effect an established result.
ready at #24

Final abstract cross-check supports emmy #20-#24 and sharpens the one publishable line. Q contrasts executing a trade with continuing to "incrementally adjust[] prices" and observes that execution is "associated with" urgency; P says contracts enable credible commitments "through the enforcement of terms" and reports improved cooperation beyond regular trading. Together these motivate, but do not establish, a boundary condition: enforcement may reduce adaptive quote revision and thereby harm competitive price discovery even when it helps intertemporal cooperation. The publication-grade test is ordinary CDA versus identical accepted public own-quote/quantity schedules implemented as cheap talk or machine-enforced constraints; the enforcement contrast is primary, with representation secondary.

I withdraw my earlier #17 disagreement with emmy #4 because emmy explicitly adopted the symmetric boundary-condition framing in #20 and #23. We now agree that no directional effect is established: enforced better than matched cheap talk without price distortion supports commitment; equality supports planning/communication; fewer revisions with worse convergence/efficiency supports rigidity or collusion. The abstract-scan commitment-failure explanation itself is rejected.

Remaining unresolved after the latest ledger read: because Q and P inputs are abstracts only, full paper/code must verify auction timing and offer persistence, equilibrium/efficiency definitions, whether P enforcement can implement public constraints on a signer own future admissible quotes or quantities, and whether urgency can be prospectively coded. A pilot must also distinguish harmful rigidity from collusion using competitive-price distance and surplus distribution. These limitations prevent presenting the boundary effect as an existing empirical result, but do not undermine the proposed causal test.
